items.title: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one id
items.content:
We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all.

I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand.

Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking.

items.title: The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude My
items.content:
The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The models attempted to complete an assignment in a setup where their normal safeguards were removed and they were deliberately given internet access. AISI reports that the models “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”.

We’re grateful to AISI for their leadership in the important discussion about how to evaluate increasingly capable AI agents. We’re working closely with them to gather more details of the incident as we conduct our own investigation. Gaining a clear picture of Claude’s understanding of its situation—by examining its reasoning transcripts and running our own analyses—will help us identify the causes of its behavior.

The prompts in the evaluation did not impose any specific restrictions on how the internet should be used. This and the removal of safeguards meant that the models were tested under “deliberately permissive conditions” that are not representative of any of our production models. Note that there was no evidence here of an escape from a secure environment.

AISI’s disclosure of the incident can be found here: https://t.co/cJ3hCBtBU7

items.title: When you work on research (particularly on long-term research), you have to accept the fact that corporate management, w
items.content:
When you work on research (particularly on long-term research), you have to accept the fact that corporate management, who is often interested in short-term impact, may think you are wasting your time and company resources. 
But it very much depends what you objectives and your horizon is.

- If your goal is keeping up with the current AI product race, then you might think that long-term bets are a waste.
- If your goal is "AGI" (whatever you mean by that) then your horizon is likely longer and your modus operandi is very different.
- However, If you think "AGI is just around the corner through LLM scaling", then you might think working on world models and other new AI concepts is a waste.
- But if you know that AGI requires a few more conceptual advances (as Demis and I do), you pick a role that maximizes progress towards that goal. That role is necessarily less connected with products, less connected with management, and more connected with research.
- I can't speak for Demis, but in my case, I've always been supportive of high-quality work on LLMs and impressed by the results. My personal interest was to advance towards human-level AI, and I never thought LLMs were the ticket. But I always thought LLMs were incredibly useful as a technology, and eventually as the centerpieces of a family of products.

As a high-level IC (not a manager), I would not have had the influence or power to stifle work on LLM even if I had wanted to (which I had not).

items.content:
Jeff Dean just left Google after 27 years to found Discovery Loop to use AI to accelerate science and engineering research.

AI will speed up drug discovery. It does not (yet) speed up making 400,000 doses and trucking them across a complex supply chain.

As I think about the next bottlenecks in AI, I think about the real world. I'm thinking about atoms, not software. Physical, tangible, gets-stuck-in-a-forklift stuff. 

In addition to cleaner and more effective energy sources, we should be looking at companies that have a headstart in manufacturing and making factories faster. Looking at Amazon and large-scale drug makers (Novartis, Pfizer, AZ, GSK, Novo Nordisk, J&J, Merck, Eli Lilly, Roche) obviously. Also at places like Flexe for warehousing, Mytra for simplification of storage, Autostore for warehouse optimization, and Berkshire Grey. This is not investment advice. 

Next decade goes to whoever can produce more (or more effectively) in the physical world.

What does an agent loop look like when it's running a piece of your business?

Build. Verify. Repeat. 

It's build, measure, learn with one change: the verify step needs a number the agent can read back.

We rank first on Google for "inbox zero." 

For "AI email assistant" we're somewhere around position 30.

So that's the loop. It runs once a month, takes one step, pushes us up, then picks it back up thirty days later.

Same on evals. I tell it the tests need to score 90 and above. It comes back at 88, adjusts the prompt, runs it again.

Same on ads. $100 a day in, profitability is the metric.

The catch is the stop condition. Without one it loops forever.

Know what "done" looks like before you start it.

items.content:
One of the best applications for agentic loops is SEO.

Here's why it works: the outcome is "black or white."

You moved up this month, you moved down, or you stayed the same.

That's the entire requirement for a loop — a metric that grades the work for you.

Build it in five parts:
1) Access. 
- Connect it to your real data, not your description of your data. 
- Google Search Console has an API. 
- DataForSEO shows you the four pages ranking above yours.

2) Action. 
- Let it audit and fix before it experiments. 
- Meta tags, JSON-LD, a missing sitemap. 
- Quick wins on most sites.

3) Memory. 
- A markdown file where it logs every change it made and why.

4) Judgment. 
- Every two weeks it reopens that file and checks its own work: I rewrote that description — did it rank us higher or lower?

5) Reversal. 
- A change that took you from position 20 to 30 gets undone. 
- Nothing here is set in stone.

Then put it on a routine so it picks up where it left off without you.

The catch: this takes months, not days. 

Months of nothing, then month four, bam bam bam, page one.

So find the number in your business that can't be argued with. 

Build the loop around that one.

items.content:
How much should you actually worry about the token cost of an agentic loop?

Two questions:
1) how thorough is each run?
2) how often does it run?

A loop that goes shallow once a month is cheap even though it never stops. 

My SEO loop costs under five dollars a run and comes back with improvements.

The value comes from the business expense it replaces. 

An SEO agency retainer is in a different order of magnitude.

The catch is your plan: 
- On a $100 or $200 max plan you're sitting on tens of thousands of dollars of usage and cost stops being a variable. 
- On $20 it's a real one, and cheaper open source models like GLM 5.2 start making sense.

Pick the monthly job you keep paying someone else to do, and have the loop ping you on Slack when it's finished.

1. Large customer growth is accelerating, not just c
items.content:
My key takeaways from the $NET (Cloudflare) Q2 2026 earnings call.

1. Large customer growth is accelerating, not just compounding off a bigger base. Customers paying $100k+/year hit 4,698, up 27% YoY, an acceleration from 25% growth last quarter. Cloudflare added 986 large customers YoY, a company record, and every cohort from $100k to $5M+ set a record for net adds. These accounts now generate 73% of revenue, up from 71% a year ago, so growth is concentrating exactly where pricing power lives.

2. Management still won't put a number on Workers revenue. Prince called Workers a meaningful revenue contributor and said the company has moved past pure adoption mode. But when Citi's Fatima Boolani directly asked for a quantitative breakout of Workers and Workers AI revenue, Prince opened with "I will start out not fully answering your question," then pivoted to anecdotes instead of a figure. Developer growth is the loudest number on the call, roughly 2 million developers added in Q2 alone versus 1.5 million for all of 2025, but investors are trusting an adjective, not a disclosed line item.

3. Guidance is deliberately fuzzy because the revenue mix is getting lumpier. Seifert told Morgan Stanley's Sanjit Singh that the shift toward pool-of-funds and consumption contracts is widening the variance between individual customers quarter to quarter, even as the multi-quarter trend stays up. Q3 guide is $736M-$737M (31% YoY) and full-year is $2.864B-$2.870B (32% YoY), both roughly in line with the current run rate rather than a step-up, despite the large-customer acceleration.

4. Restructuring costs keep growing past the original guide. Cloudflare took $151M in severance and restructuring charges in Q2 alone, $99M of it paid in cash. Full-year 2026 guidance for these charges rose to as much as $165M (versus $140M-$150M guided back in Q1), because management is prioritizing faster resolution internationally over cost control. Ex-restructuring, GAAP net loss would have been around $18M, so the "near breakeven" story only holds if you look past a cost line that's still rising.

5. Sitting out the GPU capex arms race is a real strategic bet, dressed up as discipline. Asked why Cloudflare isn't chasing GPU infrastructure contracts (a competitor disclosed a nearly $3 billion AI infra deal the same night), Prince argued that reselling commodity compute is simply worse business for Cloudflare, and claimed the company extracts roughly 10 times more utilization out of every capex dollar than hyperscalers get reselling boxes. Network capex was only 7% of revenue in Q2 versus a 14%-15% full-year target, so the bigger spend is still ahead, not behind.

6. The agentic-payments bet (Monetization Gateway, Wallets, https://t.co/XdFxFMMjP2) is a moonshot with zero disclosed revenue. Prince laid out the scale problem himself: Cloudflare handles roughly half a billion requests per second, and monetizing even 1%-10% of that through micro-transactions would require supporting 10 million to 100 million financial transactions per second, versus Visa's peak of around 20,000. That's the infrastructure bet. It's optionality on paper this quarter, not a revenue line.

7. Quiet story: security is becoming the unplanned wedge into agent infrastructure. Prince described a UK government agency that had already committed to a first-generation Zero Trust vendor, then canceled the RFP entirely once it became clear that vendor hadn't planned for securing AI agents. Partner revenue reached 31% of sales this quarter, and Prince said he expects that share to keep climbing, possibly past 50-60% over time, a channel-leverage story that gets buried under the AI headlines.

8. One dodge worth flagging: a direct question never got answered. Scotiabank's Patrick Colville asked whether rising cyber risk, the theme Prince spent the whole call describing, is already hitting the P&L in Q2 or is more of a second-half story. Seifert never circled back to it. The operator closed the call right after Prince answered the unrelated capex question. Small thing, but it's the one clean non-answer on an otherwise well-covered call.

Bottom line: management's pitch is "we're the neutral infrastructure layer for the entire agentic internet, and we're getting there while unit economics improve." The market bought it hard after hours. But the two biggest new growth stories, Workers monetization and agentic payments, both arrived without a hard number. The core business (large customers, RPO, retention) is unambiguously strong right now. The AI-native upside is still a story, not yet a line item.
